title: Words That Ask for Thinking
theme: Verbs of working with informational text
objectives: I can tell what ten task verbs ask me to do when I read and write.
I can use words such as examine, annotate, and quote to answer a reading question.
I can use the prefixes re- and de- and the ending -ize to understand words.
I can follow a set of steps to plan and write an answer.
rationale: Students cannot answer a question they cannot decode. These ten task verbs appear in classroom prompts and reading routines, and they extend the grade 3 task verbs toward annotating, quoting, and relating ideas. They sort into thinking about ideas (examine, distinguish, organize, relate), working with the text (annotate, quote, restate, decode), and going beyond it (extend, pose). Students practice each verb as an action first and then as a word in a prompt. Observe, because of, and disclose return from earlier units. The passage is a short how-to article, so the verbs are used as steps students can actually follow.

words.def: To look at something closely and carefully to learn about it.
words.ex: The doctor will examine the sprained ankle.
words.ex2: Examine each answer choice before you decide which one is correct.
words.nonExample: Glancing at something for one second is not examining it.

apps.academic: In science class, you examine a sample closely before you write what you see.
apps.spoken: Let me examine this more closely.
apps.writing: Use examine in a prompt that asks for a close look at details.

cloze.s: Before buying the used bike, Dad wanted to ___ the tires and the chain very carefully.

cloze2.s: The scientists used a magnifying glass to ___ the tiny seeds.

misuse.s: He examined the map by folding it up without ever looking at it.
misuse.why: To examine is to look closely; folding the map without looking is not examining.

visual.alt: A magnifying glass over a page.

words.def: To tell how one thing is different from another.
words.ex: Can you distinguish a frog's croak from a toad's trill?
words.ex2: It is hard to distinguish the twins unless you look closely at their freckles.
words.nonExample: Mixing two things up is the opposite of distinguishing them.

apps.academic: Readers distinguish between a fact, which can be proved, and an opinion, which cannot.
apps.spoken: I can distinguish my backpack from yours by the red zipper.
apps.writing: Use distinguish in a prompt that asks how two things differ.

cloze.s: Learning the clues helps students ___ between a fact and an opinion.

cloze2.s: From far away, it was hard to ___ a hawk from an eagle.

misuse.s: To distinguish the two coats, she decided they were exactly the same.
misuse.why: To distinguish is to tell things apart; saying they are the same does the opposite.

visual.alt: A balance scale with a magnifying glass beside it.

words.def: To put things in an order or plan that makes sense.
words.ex: Please organize your books by size on the shelf.
words.ex2: To organize her notes, Sam sorted them into four labeled folders.
words.nonExample: Tossing everything into one pile is not organizing it.

apps.academic: Writers organize ideas in a list, a chart, or an outline before they write.
apps.spoken: I need to organize my desk.
apps.writing: Use organize in a prompt that asks you to put ideas in order.

cloze.s: Before writing her report, Mia used a chart to ___ her facts into three groups.

cloze2.s: Librarians ___ the books by author so students can find them quickly.

misuse.s: He organized his closet by dumping every item in a heap on the floor.
misuse.why: To organize is to put things in order; dumping them in a heap is the opposite.

visual.alt: A tidy folder beside a neat stack of books.

words.def: To show how two ideas or things are connected.
words.ex: The author tries to relate the weather to how the character feels.
words.ex2: Can you relate what we learned about gravity to the way a ball falls?
words.nonExample: Saying cats and cookies are connected without a reason is not relating them.

apps.academic: A prompt may ask you to relate a character's choice to the problem in the story.
apps.spoken: I can relate to that story.
apps.writing: Use relate in a prompt that asks how two ideas fit together.

cloze.s: In your answer, ___ the main character's choice to what happened later in the story.

cloze2.s: Good readers ___ new facts to ideas they already know.

misuse.s: To relate the two ideas, she kept them far apart and never said how they connect.
misuse.why: To relate is to show a connection; keeping ideas apart does not.

visual.alt: A chain link beside a light bulb.

words.def: To add short notes to a text to show your thinking.
words.ex: I annotate the poem by underlining strong verbs and writing a note beside each one.
words.ex2: Please annotate the diagram with labels for each part of the plant.
words.nonExample: Reading a page without writing any notes is not annotating it.

apps.academic: Students annotate an article by underlining key ideas and writing questions in the margin.
apps.writing: Use annotate in a prompt that asks for notes on the text.

cloze.s: To ___ the article, Jo underlined key facts and wrote a question in the margin.

cloze2.s: Please ___ the map with notes that explain each stop on the trip.

misuse.s: I annotated the book by never touching it with a pencil.
misuse.why: To annotate is to add notes; never writing anything is not annotating.

visual.alt: A pencil beside a page with notes.

words.def: To repeat the exact words that someone wrote or said.
words.ex: The student will quote the first line of the poem.
words.ex2: Reporters quote people so readers can see their exact words.
words.nonExample: Telling the idea in your own words is not quoting; that is restating.

apps.academic: To support an answer, quote a short part of the text and put quotation marks around it.
apps.spoken: Can you quote the line you mean?
apps.writing: Use quote when you copy exact words as proof.

cloze.s: To prove her point, Ana will ___ one sentence from the book exactly as it is written.

cloze2.s: Put marks around the exact words when you ___ a speaker in your writing.

misuse.s: She quoted the poem by changing every word into her own.
misuse.why: To quote is to repeat exact words; changing every word is not quoting.

visual.alt: A speech bubble beside an open book.

words.def: To say something again in different words.
words.ex: Please restate the directions in your own words so I know you understand.
words.ex2: He restated the question before answering it.
words.nonExample: Copying a sentence word for word is not restating it.

apps.academic: A strong answer begins by restating the question.
apps.spoken: Let me restate that so it's clearer.
apps.writing: Use restate when you say an idea again in new words.

cloze.s: To check that she understood, Dana tried to ___ the problem in her own words.

cloze2.s: Before you answer, ___ the question so your reader knows what you are answering.

misuse.s: He restated the sentence by copying every word exactly the same.
misuse.why: To restate is to say it in different words; copying exactly is not restating.

visual.alt: A looping arrow beside a speech bubble.

words.frame: To restate the question, I say ___.

words.def: To work out what a word or message means.
words.ex: Beginning readers decode a new word by sounding out each part.
words.ex2: The spies had to decode the secret message before midnight.
words.nonExample: Guessing without looking at the letters is not decoding.

segs.m: a set of signs that hold a message

apps.academic: To decode a long word, break it into smaller parts that you know.
apps.writing: Use decode for working out a word or a hidden message.

cloze.s: Students ___ a long word by splitting it into smaller parts they know.

cloze2.s: With a secret key, the spies could ___ the hidden message.

misuse.s: She decoded the message by leaving it locked in code and never reading it.
misuse.why: To decode is to work out a message; leaving it unread is not decoding.

visual.alt: An open lock beside a row of letters.

words.frame: I decode a hard word by ___.

words.def: To make something longer or bigger or to carry it further.
words.ex: The teacher asked us to extend the pattern by three more shapes.
words.ex2: Builders will extend the road another mile to reach the new school.
words.nonExample: Cutting something shorter is not extending it.

apps.academic: A prompt may ask you to extend your answer with another reason.
apps.spoken: Can you extend the table a little?
apps.writing: Use extend when something is made longer or reaches further.

cloze.s: To ___ the pattern, the class added three more triangles to the row.

cloze2.s: The city plans to ___ the bike path to the lake next summer.

misuse.s: To extend the rope, she cut it in half and made it shorter.
misuse.why: To extend is to make longer; cutting it shorter is the opposite.

visual.alt: Arrows pointing outward beside a ruler.

words.frame: I can extend my answer by ___.

words.def: To ask a question or put forward a problem.
words.ex: Students pose questions before they start a science experiment.
words.ex2: Let me pose a riddle for the class to solve.
words.nonExample: Answering a question is not posing one.

apps.academic: Good readers pose questions about a text while they read.
apps.spoken: I'd like to pose a question.
apps.writing: Use pose for asking a question or putting forward a problem.

cloze.s: Before each experiment, scientists ___ a question they want to answer.

cloze2.s: At the start of class, the teacher will ___ a riddle for everyone to solve.

misuse.s: He posed the question by answering it and never asking anything.
misuse.why: To pose a question is to ask it; answering it is the opposite.

visual.alt: A question mark beside a raised hand.

words.frame: A question I can pose is ___.

passage.title: Tackling a Tough Reading Question
paras: Reading questions often start with a task word. If you know what the word asks you to do, you can plan your answer. Here are steps that strong readers use.
First, annotate the text. Underline important words and write short notes in the margin. Then examine the underlined parts carefully. Ask yourself what each one tells you.

Next, distinguish between the main idea and the small details. The main idea is the big point, and the details are facts that support it. Then organize your ideas in a list or a chart so you can see how they fit. You may also relate one idea to another, such as a cause to its effect.

When you write, restate the question in your own words. Then quote a short piece of the text as proof, and use quotation marks. If a word is hard to decode, break it into smaller parts or look for clues in the sentence.
Finally, extend your thinking. Pose a question of your own, such as, What would happen if the story had a different ending? Good readers never stop wondering.

qs.q: Why does the author suggest organizing ideas in a list or a chart?
choices: To see how the ideas fit together

qs.q: Why might it help to restate the question?
choices: It shows you understood what the question is asking.
It lets you skip the text.
It gives the teacher less to read.
qs.why: Saying it in your own words helps you check your understanding.

qs.q: Which sentence best explains how to prove an answer with the text?
choices: Ask yourself what each part tells you.
Pose a question of your own.
Quote a short piece of the text as proof and use quotation marks.
qs.why: Quoting with quotation marks shows exact proof from the text.

qs.q: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: Strong readers use clear steps to understand and answer questions.
Main ideas are smaller than details.
qs.why: The article gives a series of steps for tackling a question.

teacher.overview: Students learn ten task verbs that appear in classroom prompts, read a how-to article that uses each as a step, practice re-, de-, and -ize, and write answers that follow a plan.

notes.va.examine.v: Examine means look closely to learn. Contrast with glance (unit 9). Use a real object and a hand lens.
notes.va.distinguish.v: Distinguish asks how two things differ. Use pairs such as fact and opinion, or two similar animals.
notes.va.organize.v: Organize means put in an order that makes sense. Show a messy list and an organized chart side by side.
notes.va.relate.v: Relate asks how ideas connect. Provide sentence stems such as This is like ___ because ___.
notes.va.annotate.v: Annotate means add notes to show thinking. Model with a short poem and three kinds of notes: underline, question, connection.
notes.va.quote.v: Quote means copy exact words. Teach quotation marks and a lead-in such as The text says. Do not confuse with restate.
notes.va.restate.v: Re- + state. Practice with a partner: one reads a sentence, the other restates it in different words.
notes.va.decode.v: Decode a word by splitting it into parts you know. Link to the prefix de- (undo). In reading, decode also means sound out.
notes.va.extend.v: Extend means make longer or go further; in a prompt it often means add another idea. Show a pattern that grows.
notes.va.pose.v: Pose a question means to ask it. Students sometimes mix pose with answer; use a question-asking routine.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: 'The prompt says, Restate the question. Restate means to say it again in different words. The question says, Why did the heron fly away? I can restate it: What made the heron leave? Now I know what I need to answer.'
discuss: Which task word do you see most in your classroom? What does it ask you to do?
How can you disclose what you learned without copying the author's words?
misconceptions: Quote and restate mean the same thing.
Extend always means make longer; in a prompt it may mean add more thinking.
Pose means to answer a question.
extend: Create a task-word poster with a picture and a sentence for each verb.
Choose a short article and annotate it, then write a restated question and a quoted answer.
teacher.reviewAdvice: Revisit the pairs quote and restate, and examine and organize, two days later, again at one week, and reuse observe, because of, and disclose when students write full answers.

I will restate the question by saying ___.
wida.oral: Partner A gives a task word and a short text. Partner B does what the word asks and says what they did.

needsReview: Spanish glosses (reformular, plantear, descifrar, anotar, citar) not reviewed by a native speaker; reformular for restate has a more formal register than the English word.
Quote is taught only as a verb meaning to repeat exact words; the noun and the price sense are left for later.
These words are classed as function words because they act as task verbs in prompts; some grade 4 readers may need extra practice with decode in both its reading and message senses.
